newsitem.title: USA: Merck drug seen cutting heart attacks in diabetics.
newsitem.headline: Merck drug seen cutting heart attacks in diabetics.

text.p: Major coronary incidents such as heart attacks were reduced by 55 percent in people with diabetes taking simvastatin compared to those taking placebo, according to a new analysis of a study.
Simvastatin, marketed by Merck and Co Inc as Zocor, is one of a class of cholesterol-lowering drugs called statins which inhibit an enzyme that promotes the manufacture of cholesterol in the body.

A post hoc analysis of a subgroup of patients from the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study showed patients with coronary heart disease and diabetes could cut their heart-attack risk by lowering cholesterol, according to the American Diabetes Association.

In the Scandinavian Simvastin Survival Study, simvastatin was shown to reduce cardiovascular death by 42 percent and total mortality by 30 percent in the overall study population. The study tracked 4,444 patients over five years.

Kalevi Pyorala, the main author of the story, said "the benefits in terms of the number of serious heart attacks prevented was more than two times greater in diabetes than in non-diabetics with CHD because diabetic patients have a higher risk of recurrent heart attacks."
Patients with diabetes in the study reduced their total cholesterol by 27 percent, results showed.

"Although it has been widely believed by doctors that cholesterol lowering would reduce heart disease risk in people with diabetes, conclusive evidence from clinical trials was largely lacking until this new subgroup analysis of the 4S (Scandinavian Simvastin Survival Study," said Priscilla Hollander, medical director of the Ruth Collins Diabetes Center at Baylor University Medical Center in Dallas.
